modules.title: Views and Materialized Views
modules.goal: Package queries behind stable relations and choose between live and materialized results.

topics.title: What Is a View?
topics.simple: View ek saved query hai jo table ki tarah query hoti hai.
topics.pro: A view is a named stored query; it has no independent rows and is evaluated when queried.
points: Views store the query, not the data.
They can restrict columns and rows.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

topics.title: CREATE VIEW
topics.simple: CREATE VIEW se named query banao.
topics.pro: CREATE VIEW name AS query defines a view over one or more relations.
points: Column names come from the select list.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: Querying a View
topics.simple: View ko normal table ki tarah SELECT karo.
topics.pro: A view can be used in SELECT, JOIN, WHERE and most places a table is allowed.
points: Its columns are the select-list columns.
The underlying query runs each time.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM student_names ORDER BY name;

topics.title: View as Abstraction
topics.simple: View complex joins ko simple interface deta hai.
topics.pro: A view hides join and filter details behind a stable name, so consumers do not repeat fragile SQL.
points: Change the view instead of every caller.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW course_roster AS SELECT c.title, s.name FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id;

topics.title: Updatable Views
topics.simple: Simple views ko INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE kiya ja sakta hai.
topics.pro: A view is automatically updatable when it maps rows one-to-one to a base table without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations.
points: Use INSTEAD OF triggers for complex views.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: WITH CHECK OPTION
topics.simple: WITH CHECK OPTION view ke filter ke bahar writes rokta hai.
topics.pro: WITH CHECK OPTION rejects inserts or updates that would make a row invisible through the view predicate.
points: It can be LOCAL or CASCADED.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW passing AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 WITH CHECK OPTION;

topics.title: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
topics.simple: Existing view ko replace karne ke liye OR REPLACE use karo.
topics.pro: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the query in place, but cannot change existing column names, order or types.
points: Use DROP and CREATE for a redesign.

example.sql: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name, email FROM students;

topics.title: Dropping Views
topics.simple: DROP VIEW view ko remove karta hai.
topics.pro: DROP VIEW removes the named query; CASCADE also drops dependent objects, while RESTRICT refuses if dependencies exist.
points: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS is safe for scripts.

example.sql: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS student_names;

topics.title: View Dependencies
topics.simple: Views doosri views aur tables par depend kar sakti hain.
topics.pro: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping a referenced object may require CASCADE or fail with a dependency error.

example.sql: SELECT table_name FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = 'public';

topics.title: Materialized Views
topics.simple: Materialized view result ko disk par store karta hai.
topics.pro: A materialized view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but can be stale until refreshed.

example.sql: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts AS SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id;

topics.title: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW
topics.simple: Refresh stored result ko dobara compute karta hai.
topics.pro: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW reruns the query and replaces the stored rows.
points: It locks the view by default.

example.sql: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts;

topics.title: Concurrent Refresh
topics.simple: CONCURRENTLY refresh ke dauraan reads allow karta hai.
topics.pro: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and avoids blocking readers, at the cost of more work.
points: Cannot run inside a transaction block.

example.sql:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX course_counts_course_id ON course_counts (course_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY course_counts;

topics.title: Indexing Materialized Views
topics.simple: Materialized view par index laga sakte hain.
topics.pro: Because a materialized view stores rows, it supports ordinary indexes for lookup and uniqueness.
points: A unique index enables concurrent refresh.

example.sql: CREATE INDEX course_counts_total ON course_counts (total DESC);

topics.title: View vs Materialized View
topics.simple: View live hota hai; materialized view cached hota hai.
topics.pro: A view always reflects current base data, while a materialized view reflects the last refresh and can be stale.
points: Materialized views trade freshness for speed.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM course_counts;

topics.title: Security with Views
topics.simple: View se column-level access restrict kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Granting access to a view can expose only selected columns and rows without granting the base table.
points: Views do not bypass underlying privileges unless security definer is used.

example.sql: GRANT SELECT ON student_names TO app_role;

topics.title: Performance of Views
topics.simple: View apne aap me optimization cache nahi hai.
topics.pro: A plain view is expanded into the caller query and optimized with it; it does not store results or guarantee a fixed plan.
points: The planner sees through simple views.
Complex views can still be expensive.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM high_scorers;
example.output: A plan over the students table.

topics.title: Common View Errors
topics.simple: Duplicate columns, bad replacements aur stale materialized data common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are duplicate output names, replacing a view with an incompatible shape, refreshing without a unique index and forgetting that a materialized view is stale.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id AS student_id, c.id AS course_id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;

topics.title: Practical Reporting View
topics.simple: Reporting view stable columns aur filters deta hai.
topics.pro: A reporting view joins and labels data once, giving dashboards a stable interface over changing tables.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW enrollment_report AS SELECT c.title AS course, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

topics.title: Column Aliases in Views
topics.simple: View columns ko explicit names do.
topics.pro: Explicit aliases prevent duplicate names and keep the view contract stable when the underlying query changes.
points: Column order is part of the contract.

example.sql: CREATE VIEW student_labels AS SELECT id AS student_id, name AS display_name FROM students;

topics.title: View Maintenance
topics.simple: Views ko schema changes ke saath maintain karo.
topics.pro: Review dependencies, test replacements and refresh materialized views after data changes.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM pg_depend WHERE refobjid = 'students'::regclass;

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain What Is a View? in a production query.
interview.answer: A view is a named stored query; it has no independent rows and is evaluated when queried. Key rules: Views store the query, not the data. They simplify complex SQL. They can restrict columns and rows.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain CREATE VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE VIEW name AS query defines a view over one or more relations. Key rules: Name the view. The query follows AS. Column names come from the select list.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Querying a View in a production query.
interview.answer: A view can be used in SELECT, JOIN, WHERE and most places a table is allowed. Key rules: Query it by name. Its columns are the select-list columns. The underlying query runs each time.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View as Abstraction in a production query.
interview.answer: A view hides join and filter details behind a stable name, so consumers do not repeat fragile SQL. Key rules: Centralize reusable logic. Expose only needed columns. Change the view instead of every caller.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Updatable Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A view is automatically updatable when it maps rows one-to-one to a base table without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations. Key rules: Simple projections are updatable. Aggregates block updates. Use INSTEAD OF triggers for complex views.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain WITH CHECK OPTION in a production query.
interview.answer: WITH CHECK OPTION rejects inserts or updates that would make a row invisible through the view predicate. Key rules: It protects the view contract. It applies to writes. It can be LOCAL or CASCADED.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the query in place, but cannot change existing column names, order or types. Key rules: It keeps dependencies. Column shape must stay compatible. Use DROP and CREATE for a redesign.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Dropping Views in a production query.
interview.answer: DROP VIEW removes the named query; CASCADE also drops dependent objects, while RESTRICT refuses if dependencies exist. Key rules: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS is safe for scripts. CASCADE can remove dependents. The base tables remain.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View Dependencies in a production query.
interview.answer: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping a referenced object may require CASCADE or fail with a dependency error. Key rules: Check dependencies before dropping. CASCADE is destructive. information_schema.views lists definitions.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Materialized Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A materialized view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but can be stale until refreshed. Key rules: It stores rows. It must be refreshed. It can have indexes.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW in a production query.
interview.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW reruns the query and replaces the stored rows. Key rules: It can be expensive. It locks the view by default. CONCURRENTLY reduces blocking.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Concurrent Refresh in a production query.
interview.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and avoids blocking readers, at the cost of more work. Key rules: Requires a unique index. Cannot run inside a transaction block. It may be slower.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Indexing Materialized Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Because a materialized view stores rows, it supports ordinary indexes for lookup and uniqueness. Key rules: Index the refreshed rows. A unique index enables concurrent refresh. Refresh maintains the indexes.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View vs Materialized View in a production query.
interview.answer: A view always reflects current base data, while a materialized view reflects the last refresh and can be stale. Key rules: Views have no refresh cost. Materialized views trade freshness for speed. Choose by freshness requirements.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Security with Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Granting access to a view can expose only selected columns and rows without granting the base table. Key rules: Grant on the view. Do not expose sensitive columns. Views do not bypass underlying privileges unless security definer is used.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Performance of Views in a production query.
interview.answer: A plain view is expanded into the caller query and optimized with it; it does not store results or guarantee a fixed plan. Key rules: The planner sees through simple views. Complex views can still be expensive. Materialize only when needed.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Common View Errors in a production query.
interview.answer: Common failures are duplicate output names, replacing a view with an incompatible shape, refreshing without a unique index and forgetting that a materialized view is stale. Key rules: Alias duplicate columns. Keep replacement shapes compatible. Refresh materialized views.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Practical Reporting View in a production query.
interview.answer: A reporting view joins and labels data once, giving dashboards a stable interface over changing tables. Key rules: Name columns explicitly. Keep the grain clear. Document refresh expectations.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain Column Aliases in Views in a production query.
interview.answer: Explicit aliases prevent duplicate names and keep the view contract stable when the underlying query changes. Key rules: Alias expressions. Alias duplicate names. Column order is part of the contract.

interview.q: Module 17 · Explain View Maintenance in a production query.
interview.answer: Review dependencies, test replacements and refresh materialized views after data changes. Key rules: Track dependent views. Test CREATE OR REPLACE. Schedule refreshes.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Updatable Views matter?
logic.answer: A view is automatically updatable when it maps rows one-to-one to a base table without aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY or set operations. Simple projections are updatable. Aggregates block updates. Use INSTEAD OF triggers for complex views.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does WITH CHECK OPTION matter?
logic.answer: WITH CHECK OPTION rejects inserts or updates that would make a row invisible through the view predicate. It protects the view contract. It applies to writes. It can be LOCAL or CASCADED.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW matter?
logic.answer: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the query in place, but cannot change existing column names, order or types. It keeps dependencies. Column shape must stay compatible. Use DROP and CREATE for a redesign.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Dropping Views matter?
logic.answer: DROP VIEW removes the named query; CASCADE also drops dependent objects, while RESTRICT refuses if dependencies exist. DROP VIEW IF EXISTS is safe for scripts. CASCADE can remove dependents. The base tables remain.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does View Dependencies matter?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL tracks dependencies, so dropping a referenced object may require CASCADE or fail with a dependency error. Check dependencies before dropping. CASCADE is destructive. information_schema.views lists definitions.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Materialized Views matter?
logic.answer: A materialized view stores the query result physically, so reads are fast but can be stale until refreshed. It stores rows. It must be refreshed. It can have indexes.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW matter?
logic.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW reruns the query and replaces the stored rows. It can be expensive. It locks the view by default. CONCURRENTLY reduces blocking.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Concurrent Refresh matter?
logic.answer: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and avoids blocking readers, at the cost of more work. Requires a unique index. Cannot run inside a transaction block. It may be slower.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Indexing Materialized Views matter?
logic.answer: Because a materialized view stores rows, it supports ordinary indexes for lookup and uniqueness. Index the refreshed rows. A unique index enables concurrent refresh. Refresh maintains the indexes.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does View vs Materialized View matter?
logic.answer: A view always reflects current base data, while a materialized view reflects the last refresh and can be stale. Views have no refresh cost. Materialized views trade freshness for speed. Choose by freshness requirements.

logic.q: Module 17 · Why does Security with Views matter?
logic.answer: Granting access to a view can expose only selected columns and rows without granting the base table. Grant on the view. Do not expose sensitive columns. Views do not bypass underlying privileges unless security definer is used.

debug.title: Duplicate view columns
debug.broken: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id, c.id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;
debug.fix: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.id AS student_id, c.id AS course_id FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;
debug.expected: A view with two distinct columns.

debug.title: View already exists
debug.broken: CREATE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;
debug.fix: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW high_scorers AS SELECT id, name FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

debug.title: Concurrent refresh without index
debug.fix:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX course_counts_course_id ON course_counts (course_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY course_counts;

debug.title: Drop with dependency
debug.error: cannot drop view because other objects depend on it
debug.expected: The view and dependents are removed.

debug.title: Check option violation
debug.broken:
CREATE VIEW passing AS SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 WITH CHECK OPTION;
INSERT INTO passing (name, marks) VALUES ('Zara', 40);
debug.error: new row violates check option for view "passing"

debug.title: Stale materialized view
debug.fix:
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW course_counts;
SELECT * FROM course_counts;
debug.error: The counts are from the last refresh

debug.title: Replace changes column
debug.broken: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name, email FROM students;
debug.fix:
DROP VIEW student_names;
CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name, email FROM students;
debug.error: cannot change name of view column "name"

debug.title: Wrong grant target
debug.broken: GRANT SELECT ON students TO app_role;
debug.fix: GRANT SELECT ON student_names TO app_role;
debug.error: The role can read sensitive base columns
debug.expected: Only the view columns are exposed.

debug.title: View after drop
debug.fix:
CREATE VIEW student_names AS SELECT id, name FROM students;
SELECT * FROM student_names;

revision.q: Module 17 · State one key rule for What Is a View?.
revision.answer: Views store the query, not the data.
